article.content: Follow the day’s news live Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The Victorian Greens will today announce an election commitment to establish a lobbyist register and ban political donations from “big corporate money”. The party said under their plan, there would be a legislated register for lobbyists with teeth and a total ban on political donations from the gambling industry, fossil fuel companies and property developers. These corporations don’t hand over thousands of dollars out of the goodness of their hearts. They expect something in return, and it’s everyday Victorians who end up paying the price. They’ve both dealt with male-dominated industries with cultures that are pretty rough and challenging for women, and so they’re perfect people to lead that cultural journey. Continue reading...

The Victorian Greens are set to unveil a major electoral pledge aimed at overhauling political funding and transparency across the state, according to a report published by World news | The Guardian. Under the proposed platform, the party will commit to creating a formal lobbyist register alongside a strict prohibition on political donations originating from large corporate entities. The initiative highlights ongoing tensions over campaign finance and the influence of money in Australian elections, a theme mirrored in broader national debates detailed in our previous [Australia politics live coverage](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/australia-politics-live-mps-to-pay-tribute-to-helen-haines-as-parliament).

## Campaign Finance and Transparency Reforms

According to the source material, the forthcoming announcement by the Victorian Greens forms part of their broader strategy to curb the political leverage wielded by corporate donors. By pushing for a mandatory lobbyist register, the party aims to increase public scrutiny over political access and influence. While the Greens argue that these measures are essential for restoring public trust in democratic institutions, critics and major political parties often contend that such sweeping bans could disadvantage smaller parties or restrict legitimate political participation.

Political donation reform has long been a contentious issue within the [Australian political landscape](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/australian-judge-rejects-prisoner-s-human-rights-challenge-to-vegemite-ban), with successive governments grappling with how to balance transparency against the practical costs of campaigning. Public debates frequently pit advocates for rigorous disclosure against those who argue that existing frameworks are sufficient to prevent corruption. 

## Context and Stakes

The stakes surrounding campaign finance reform involve the fundamental integrity of democratic representation and public perception of government accountability. When voters perceive that wealthy corporations hold disproportionate sway over policymakers, disillusionment grows, potentially driving engagement toward minor parties or independent candidates who champion systemic change. For minor parties like the Greens, pushing these reforms serves both a policy goal and a distinct electoral positioning strategy to attract voters dissatisfied with the major parties.

## What to Watch

Observers will be tracking the formal policy rollout to see the specific enforcement mechanisms proposed by the Greens, as well as the reactions from Labor and the Coalition. Future developments may also reveal whether other crossbench or minor parties choose to adopt similar anti-corporate donation platforms ahead of the upcoming electoral cycle.

Sources: [World news | The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/live/2026/oct/27/one-nation-pauline-hanson-independent-jacqui-lambie-labor-anthony-albanese-coalition-ntwnfb)
